summary:
Arora bridges manual kernel fundamentals to LLM evaluation. She details three intra-GPU transfer mechanisms: the host-initiated copy engine (large bulk messages), the device-initiated Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) (saturating NVLink with small messages, few registers), and register-level PTX load/store instructions (uniquely exploiting NVSwitch in-network reductions). Each presents distinct register, SM-utilization, and in-network-computation trade-offs.

Two compute/communication overlap schedules follow. Intra-SM schedules assign compute and communication warps within one processor, requiring aligned patterns. Inter-SM schedules dedicate separate processors to compute, communication, and memory—better for misaligned patterns and maximizing NVLink traversal. ParallelKittens encapsulates these primitives; roughly a dozen extra lines convert a single-GPU kernel into a multi-GPU one, achieving state-of-the-art results across data, sequence, and expert parallelism in production at Together AI and Cursor.

Turning to LLM evaluation, ParallelKernelBench presents models with an unoptimized PyTorch+torch.distributed reference and a system topology, asking for a CUDA kernel using unified virtual addressing. Eighty-seven problems span combinatorial parallelism dimensions drawn from real GitHub repositories. Pass@K and fast-one@K metrics show the best frontier model solves 28/87 zero-shot with 22 faster than baseline; scaling plateaus fast-one@K near 31%. A multi-turn agent harness lifted solves from 24 to 35 with 26 ≥1× faster. Successes cluster in internet-representative patterns; failures involve collective ordering, partitioning, scheduling, and transfer-mechanism choice. Net-new production kernels emerged (NeMo vocab-parallel, Hyena CP, SAM 3 IOU suppression). Arora closes by urging research that grows with networking trends—larger scale-up domains, reduced scale-out, and massive on-chip memory—inviting contact via email.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Multi-GPU kernel design hinges on choosing among three transfer mechanisms—copy engine (bulk), TMA (small messages), and register-level (in-network reduction)—each with distinct register, SM, and NVSwitch trade-offs.
Two overlap schedules exist: intra-SM (aligned patterns) and inter-SM (misaligned patterns, NVLink traversal); GEM+reduce+scatter favors intra-SM while GEM+all-reduce favors inter-SM with NVSwitch.
ParallelKittens adds roughly a dozen lines to a single-GPU kernel and achieves state-of-the-art data, sequence, and expert parallelism in production at Together AI and Cursor.
ParallelKernelBench spans 87 problems from real GitHub repositories across combinatorial parallelism dimensions to ensure production relevance.

Best frontier models solve only 28/87 zero-shot with 22 faster than PyTorch+NCCL; scaling samples plateaus fast-one@K near 31%, and a multi-turn agent harness lifts solves to 35/87 with 26 ≥1× faster.

Model failures are not CUDA syntax but reasoning over collective ordering, data partitioning, intra-vs-inter-SM scheduling, and transfer-mechanism choice; successes cluster in internet-representative patterns.
Speedups come mainly from eliminating NCCL staging overhead in favor of direct NVLink loads/stores once correctness is established.
Future research must grow with networking trends: larger scale-up domains, reduced scale-out, and massive on-chip memory structures.

sections.title: Introduction and motivation: bottleneck shift to multi-GPU communication
sections.summary: Arora introduces herself (Together AI, formerly Stanford Hazy Research, incoming Caltech professor) and frames the talk around simplifying multi-GPU AI kernels. Single-GPU optimizations and DSLs have moved the bottleneck to multi-GPU communication. She previews the five-part agenda and the ParallelKernelBench benchmark.

sections.title: GPU hardware primer: SMs, caches, HBM, and memory distance
sections.summary: Using an H100 die image, Arora explains rainbow-colored SMs, L2 rectangles, and HBM black boxes, then walks up the memory hierarchy. Registers are closest/fastest (~130 TB/s) but tiny; HBM is large but slow. Threads are grouped into blocks and scheduled onto SMs, with CPU-side memory also visible across the system.

sections.title: Interconnect hierarchy: PCIe, NVLink, NVSwitch, InfiniBand
sections.summary: She maps the multi-GPU interconnect stack: PCIe for CPU↔GPU, InfiniBand/TCP for inter-node, and NVLink + NVSwitch for intra-node. NVSwitch forms a non-blocking fabric enabling GPU↔GPU communication and in-network acceleration for primitives like multicast and reductions.

sections.title: Why GPU networking, why now: scale, disaggregation, and vendor diversity
sections.summary: AI workloads now span 72- to 576-GPU scale-up domains, KV cache across GPU/CPU/disk/remote, and disaggregated prefill/decode/speculative steps. Vendor networking stacks diverge: AMD XGMI point-to-point, TPU 3D torus with optical wraparound, and Nvidia NVLink (~900 GB/s) plus NVSwitch with tensor-memory acceleration.

sections.title: Compute vs. communication scaling and the roofline gap
sections.summary: A100→B200 delivered 7.2× BF16 tensor-core throughput, but intra-node comm only 3× and inter-node 2×. NCCL/RCCL are tuned for bulk contiguous transfers and force synchronization, breaking on fine-grained or fused collectives. Across ParallelKernelBench, PyTorch+NCCL baselines land below 50% of the communication-aware roofline.

sections.title: Compilers, DSLs, and hand-tuned operators fall short
sections.summary: Frameworks like Megatron-LM, FlexFlow, and Nanoflow orchestrate bulk collectives via NCCL. Compilers/DSLs such as Triton Distributed and Tilelang struggle to keep pace with hardware changes. Hand-tuned operators achieve peak performance but take ~5–6 months to retune per precision.

sections.title: Research question and ParallelKittens primitives
sections.summary: Arora poses the central research question and introduces ParallelKittens—a small set of minimal primitives and patterns built by hand to study multi-GPU kernel fundamentals.

sections.title: Transfer mechanisms: copy engine, TMA, and register-level instructions
sections.summary: Arora details three intra-GPU data-transfer mechanisms. The host-initiated copy engine handles large bulk messages. The device-initiated TMA saturates NVLink with small messages using few registers and processors. Register-level PTX load/store instructions enable NVSwitch in-network reductions but consume precious registers.

sections.title: Compute/communication overlap: intra-SM vs inter-SM schedules
sections.summary: Two main overlap schedules exist. Intra-SM schedules assign compute and communication warps within a single processor, requiring patterns to align. Inter-SM schedules dedicate separate processors to compute, communication, and memory—better for misaligned patterns and maximizing NVLink traversal.

sections.title: ParallelKittens in production
sections.summary: ParallelKittens encapsulates transfer mechanisms, overlap schedules, and buffering/synchronization control into simple primitives. Roughly a dozen lines extend a single-GPU kernel into a multi-GPU one, achieving state-of-the-art results in production at Together AI and Cursor.

sections.title: ParallelKernelBench: 87 problems across combinatorial parallelism dimensions
sections.summary: Each task presents the model with an unoptimized PyTorch+torch.distributed reference and a system topology, asking for a CUDA kernel using unified virtual addressing. Eighty-seven problems are drawn from real GitHub repositories across combinatorial parallelism dimensions.

sections.title: Frontier model results: zero-shot, scaling, and agent harness
sections.summary: Pass@K and fast-one@K metrics show the best frontier model solves 28/87 zero-shot with 22 faster than baseline. Scaling samples lifts correctness to 36 but plateaus fast-one@K near 31%. A multi-turn agent harness lifted solves from 24 to 35/87 with 26 ≥1× faster, but performance plateaued.

sections.title: Lessons and net-new production kernels
sections.summary: Arora concludes that a small set of patterns governs effective intra-GPU kernels, but models currently cannot reason through the trade-offs. She highlights net-new kernels already produced: NeMo vocab-parallel filtering, Hyena context parallelism, and SAM 3 video segmentation IOU suppression.

sections.title: Closing remarks: growing with evolving networking trends
sections.summary: Arora closes by urging research that grows with networking trends—larger scale-up domains, a shift away from scale-out, and massive on-chip memory structures—and invites contact via email.

limitations: Copy engine cannot saturate NVLink with small messages; TMA cannot leverage NVSwitch in-network computations; register-level instructions consume scarce registers and SM resources.
Intra-SM overlap requires compute and communication patterns to align; misalignment forces costly inter-SM schedules.
Frontier models plateau at ~31% fast-one@K on ParallelKernelBench as samples scale.
Multi-turn agent harness improvements plateau with additional compute; further techniques are required.
Models frequently fail to use register-level transfer instructions or TMA when writing kernels.
Model successes are concentrated in internet-representative patterns rather than novel reasoning.
